### sync

Fetch and sync a set of repos to their remotes in one atomic operation: fetch, converge the
bookmark, reposition `@`. With no flags the repo set is `.`, the one repo `sync` is run in, whichever
side of a workspace that is. Name a side or both with `-s` / `--scope`, or point at a different
workspace root or single repo with `-R` / `--repo`. Verify-then-act happens inside a single
invocation against one fetch snapshot, since a separate check-then-apply pair of runs would race
the remote. A look with `--dry-run` is not that check: a sync after it verifies again.

Per repo, `sync` classifies the local bookmark, as it was before the fetch, against its remote:

| State | Meaning | Action |
|------|---------|--------|
| up-to-date | local == remote | none |
| behind | local is ancestor of remote | `jj bookmark set <b> -r <b>@<remote>` |
| ahead | remote is ancestor of local | none (push is a separate step) |
| diverged | neither is ancestor | on a go, `jj rebase -b <local-head> -d <b>@<remote>` |
| no remote | bookmark has no `@<remote>` counterpart | none, skip |

The bookmark is read before the fetch because the fetch is not a look: jj's `git fetch` moves a
tracked bookmark that is behind to the remote's, and leaves one that diverged conflicted. Where the
bookmark was is what "as found" means, and two paths put it back there:

- **`--dry-run`** looks only. It fetches, reports each repo's state and what a sync would do, and
  moves no bookmark and no `@`. The remote-tracking refs (`<b>@<remote>`) are what it updates. It
  exits 0 whenever the look itself succeeded, whatever it found.
- **A diverged bookmark is rebased only on a go**: `--rebase`, or a yes at the prompt on a
  terminal. With neither, the bookmark is left as found, the other repos still sync, and the run
  then exits non-zero naming the repo, so a `--quiet` caller learns it was not synced.

`--bookmark` names a **work-repo** bookmark only: the bot repo is a linear journal on `main` by
design, so its side of every step (tracking preflight, classify, act, reposition) always uses `main`
regardless of the flag.

After the bookmark action above, `sync` repositions `@` onto the freshly-synced bookmark as a final
pass, run after every repo syncs cleanly. The rule differs by repo (`@-` is the parent of `@`, `<b>`
is the synced `--bookmark`):

- **Work repo** (the workspace root):
  - `@` is clean (empty) and `<b>` sits ahead of `@-` on the same line -> `jj new <b>` starts a
    fresh `@` on the new tip (the old empty `@` is auto-abandoned).
  - `@` has changes -> `sync` asks before moving it, and `--rebase` answers yes up front (`jj
    rebase -b @ -d <b>`). Declining, or not being a TTY with no `--rebase`, leaves `@` in place and
    says so.
  - `@` already sits on `<b>`, or `<b>` isn't on `@-`'s line (diverged / `@` ahead) -> `@` is left
    untouched, with a note why.
- **Bot repo** (`.claude`): no-op when `@-` is already the `main` tip, so `@` keeps its change id
  and any live session writes stay in the working copy. When `main` moved, `jj new main` starts a
  fresh empty `@` on the new tip, and the prior `@` (e.g. `/exit`'s trailing session writes) is
  preserved as a sibling head. If `@-` isn't on `main`, `sync` errors rather than strand it.

On any failure during fetch/classify/act/reposition (conflicted rebase, subprocess error, anything)
`sync` **stops where the failing step stopped**. Nothing is auto-reverted, so the state can be
inspected as-is (jj's operation log holds everything, so nothing is lost by stopping). Before
acting, sync captures each repo's pre-sync `jj op` id in memory, and the failure report lists
every repo's op id. The undo is explicit, per repo: `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`. Nothing
persists across
invocations: a snapshot that outlives its run is a stale target waiting to rewind unrelated work.
That is also why the former `revert` subcommand was removed at 0.78.3: it restored the persisted
snapshot with no guard against discarding operations recorded after the failed sync. A safer
revert would derive its target from the op log and refuse when unrelated operations sit in
between. Until such a design exists, `jj op log` + `jj op restore` is the recovery.

```
vc-x1 sync                            # the repo in the current directory
vc-x1 sync --dry-run                  # look only: report, and move nothing
vc-x1 sync --rebase                   # rebase a diverged bookmark or a dirty @ without asking
vc-x1 sync --scope=work               # only the work repo
vc-x1 sync --scope=agent              # only the agent repo
vc-x1 sync --scope=both               # both repos of a dual workspace

Making `--dry-run` the default is a reasonable choice, and cheap to do now since nothing is pushed. How I see it:

**For a dry-run default**
- **One rule for a neophyte:** sync never changes anything unless you say so.
- **It matches the repair commands.** `fix-desc`, `fix-todo` and `agent-files size` already look by default and take `--no-dry-run` to act.
- **The rules get simpler.** Acquaint and Opening can name the bare `vc-x1 sync --scope=both`, with no flag to forget.

- **A look is not risk-free either.** It still fetches and then restores. In the agent-repo under a live session, if the working copy changes during that fraction of a second, sync cannot restore and leaves the fetched state with the manual undo printed. That gap is the same for a look and for a sync, so the default doesn't close it.

**My view:** I recommended keeping the acting default earlier, and with this rung's safety I still think it is defensible. But if you're uneasy, the dry-run default is the more conservative choice and costs only keystrokes, so I'd go with your lean.

- `--no-dry-run` makes sync act; a bare sync looks.

content.text:
Yes, it can always tell the user how to restore, and your nervousness has some basis. Here is the honest picture.

**Can it instruct instead of restoring?**

Yes. Sync notes each repo's operation before it touches anything, so on a failure it can stop and print the exact way back. That is what `--keep` does now, and what sync did before this rung.

One catch I found today: the raw `jj op restore <op>` it prints is not a complete undo of a fetch. It leaves jj unable to see the remote's change on the next fetch, so the repo reports "up to date" when it isn't. The instruction should point at our own restore, which is exactly what the `--undo` rung would provide: "run `vc-x1 sync --undo` to put it back".

**Can an automatic restore make things worse?**

Nothing can be lost: a restore is itself a jj operation, and everything before it stays in the operation log. But it can confuse, in three ways:
- **It is new code.** The restore reaches into git's refs directly. It has tests, but it is a day old.
- **It can fail half-way.** If it resets git's refs and then fails to restore jj's view, the two disagree until the next fetch. I can order the steps so a half-failure looks like "the fetch happened again", which jj handles natively, but I can't make it impossible.
- **It acts when the user isn't looking.** After a failed rebase, a person may want to see the conflict, not find it silently gone.

**What I'd suggest: restore only sync's own look, never an act you asked for**

- **Bare `vc-x1 sync` looks** (your dry-run default). It fetches, reports, and restores. That restore is unavoidable: with jj a fetch is not a look, so a look that didn't restore would leave the repo changed.
- **A sync that declines to act** restores the same way. That covers a diverged repo with no `--rebase`: sync did nothing but look.
- **A sync you told to act, that fails part-way, stops.** It leaves the state where it is and prints one line: what failed, and `vc-x1 sync --undo` to go back. No automatic rewind.
- **`--keep` goes away**, since keeping the state becomes the behaviour on failure.

So the rule a neophyte learns is: sync changes nothing unless told to; when told to and it fails, it stops and tells you the one command that undoes it.

This is closer to how sync behaved before today, which the project chose deliberately when `revert` was removed, with a correct undo added on top.

**The cost:** `--undo` becomes necessary for the failure path, not just a convenience, so rung 2 has to land with rung 1. That fits the three-commit plan.

Do you want that: dry-run by default, restore only after a look or a declined act, and stop-and-instruct on a failed act?

content.text:
Both are real, and together they point at a different design: a look that never touches the repo at all, so there is nothing to restore.

**On losing conversation**

You're right to worry. The agent-repo's working copy is this conversation, being written as we speak. A restore resets files on disk to an earlier state. I built a guard for that: if anything was written while sync ran, it refuses to restore. But the guard has a gap of a few milliseconds between its check and the restore, and a transcript line landing in that gap would be gone from disk. Small odds, but the worst possible thing to lose, and it would happen on the most routine command.

**On the user running it alone**

That argues for a command with no hidden steps: nothing that fetches and then quietly rewinds, and no failure state that needs me to interpret.

**What I'd do instead: ask the remote, don't fetch**

The reason a look needed a restore is that with jj a fetch changes the repo. So don't fetch. Git can ask a remote "what commit is your `main` on?" without downloading or changing anything. Comparing that answer with what the repo already knows gives:

| Remote's `main` is | Local `main` | Report |
|---|---|---|
| the same commit as local | any | up to date |
| unchanged since the last fetch | has unpushed commits | ahead |
| new, and local has no unpushed commits | at the last-fetched commit | behind: a sync will follow the remote |
| new, and local has unpushed commits | ahead of the last-fetched commit | diverged |

Then the whole command becomes:
- **`vc-x1 sync` (the default): a true look.** No fetch, no jj operation, no file touched, so no restore. Safe in the agent-repo mid-conversation and safe for anyone to run.
- **`vc-x1 sync --no-dry-run`: act.** It looks first, the same read-only way. Diverged without `--rebase` is refused before anything is fetched. Otherwise it fetches and syncs.
- **If the act fails part-way, it stops** and prints what happened and `vc-x1 sync --undo`. Nothing is rewound automatically.
- **`vc-x1 sync --undo`: the only place a restore runs**, asked for by a person, with the live-writer guard.

**What this gives up**
- **Less detail in the look.** Without downloading, it can't tell "behind" from "the remote rewrote a commit", and it can't predict a conflict. It says "the remote has moved and you have nothing unpushed", which is enough for an acquaint and a cycle start.
- **One piece to verify.** I need to confirm the cleanest way to ask the remote from our code. jj's own fetch already runs `git` underneath, so the ability is there, but I haven't checked how it's exposed.

**What it does to today's work**
- The restore code and its tests stay, but move behind `--undo`.
- The automatic restores, the `--keep` flag, and the fetch-then-restore look come out.
- The "rewritten" handling and the read-the-bookmark-before-fetch classification stay for the acting path.

I think this is the simplest version yet, and it answers both of your points directly: the routine command cannot lose anything because it changes nothing. If you want it, I'll first check how to ask the remote without fetching, and bring that back before rewriting the rung.

content.text:
Yes, I think that is the right idea, and it is simpler than everything I've built today. If the repo holds no local work, a fetch has nothing of yours to damage, so there is nothing to restore.

**Why your three checks make a fetch safe**

Everything dangerous we found needs local work to collide with:
- **Diverged** needs local commits the remote doesn't have. "All bookmarks fast-forward only" rules that out.
- **A conflict from a rewritten remote** needs edits in `@`. "`@` is empty" rules that out.
- **Commits under `@` being rebased** needs `@-` to be local-only. "`@-` is a commit on the remote" rules that out.

With all three true, the only things a fetch can do are move a bookmark forward, follow a rewrite, and move an empty `@`. And you're right about restoring: every commit involved is already on the remote, so "going back" is just pointing at the older commit. Sync can print "main: old → new" and that line is the whole undo.

I'd make the third check a little stronger: no local-only commit with content anywhere in the repo, not just on bookmarks. A stray unbookmarked change sitting on a rewritten commit would be rebased too.

**What sync does when the checks fail**

It does not fetch. It reports what local work it found (uncommitted changes in `@`, commits not on the remote, a bookmark that is ahead) and says how to proceed: push the work, or pass `--rebase` to go ahead anyway. Only that forced path can fail part-way, and there it stops and tells the user what to do.

**The one wrinkle: the agent-repo**

Its `@` is never empty while a session is running, because the conversation is being written into it. So under your checks sync would never fetch the agent-repo mid-session. But it does need syncing at the start of a session on a second machine, or the first push is rejected.

I'd exempt the agent-repo's `@` from the "empty" check and keep the other two. The remaining risk is narrow: another machine rewrote the tip and touched the same session file as this conversation. In that one case sync would stop, not restore, so the conversation's files are never rewound.

**What this replaces**
- No dry-run default is needed: the bare command is safe by construction, because it only acts when there is nothing to hurt.
- No automatic restore, no `--keep`, no live-writer guard. Most of today's restore code comes out.
- `--undo` shrinks to the forced path. I'd question whether it is still worth a rung, or whether a printed instruction is enough.

**What it doesn't tell you**

When the checks fail, sync reports the local work but doesn't contact the remote, so it can't say whether the remote has also moved. An acquaint would learn "ahead" or "uncommitted work", not "diverged". Asking the remote without fetching could add that later.

Do you want me to rework the rung this way: gate the fetch on those checks, with the agent-repo's `@` exempt?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Acceptance check for the first rung of `feat: sync is safe by default`:
# a repo is fetched only when it holds no local work.
set -uo pipefail
d="$1"
rm -rf "$d"
mkdir -p "$d"
cd "$d" || exit 1
git init -q --bare remote.git
jj git clone --quiet remote.git a
(cd a && echo one > f && jj commit --quiet -m one && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @- \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
for n in b c r1 r2; do jj git clone --quiet remote.git "$n"; done
(cd a && echo two > g && jj commit --quiet -m two && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @- \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
(cd c && echo local > h && jj commit --quiet -m local && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @-)

show() { jj log -R "$1" --ignore-working-copy -r 'main | @- | main@origin' --no-graph \
  -T 'commit_id.short(8) ++ " " ++ if(conflict, "CONFLICT ", "") ++ bookmarks ++ " " ++ remote_bookmarks ++ " | " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'; }
run() { echo "\$ vc-x1 sync $*"; vc-x1-dev --no-banner sync "$@" < /dev/null; echo "exit=$?"; }

echo "=== behind, no local work"; show b; run -R b; show b
echo "=== diverged (an unpushed commit)"; show c; run -R c; show c
echo "=== diverged, on the go"; run -R c --rebase; show c

# The remote rewrites its tip. r1 holds no local work, r2 an edit to the same file.
jj git fetch --quiet -R r1; jj new --quiet main -R r1
jj git fetch --quiet -R r2; jj new --quiet main -R r2
(cd a && echo rewritten > g && jj squash --quiet --ignore-immutable \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
echo "r2-local-edit" > r2/g
echo "=== rewritten, no local work"; show r1; run -R r1; show r1
echo "=== rewritten under an edited file"; show r2; run -R r2; show r2; echo "--- r2/g: $(cat r2/g)"

content.text:
The rung is reworked around your gate, and full validation passes (all four commands, 708 tests). Nothing is pushed beyond the empty `feat-sync-is-safe-by-default` bookmark.

**What sync does now**

Before fetching a repo, sync checks for local work:
- uncommitted changes in `@` (not asked of the agent-repo, whose `@` is the running session)
- an `@-` that is not on the remote
- a bookmark with commits the remote does not have

A repo with none of these is fetched and synced as before. A repo with any of them is not fetched at all. Sync lists what it found, syncs the other repos, and exits non-zero. `--rebase` is the go to sync it anyway.

**What came out:** `--dry-run`, `--keep`, the automatic restores, the live-writer guard, and the y/N prompt on a terminal. Nothing is ever rewound by the routine command.

**What stayed from earlier drafts:** the bookmark is read before the fetch, a "rewritten" state for a remote that replaced a commit, and an ahead bookmark is reported.

**Acceptance, run in scratch clones with the built `vc-x1-dev`**

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Behind, no local work | fetched and fast-forwarded, exit 0 |
| Unpushed commit on `main` | not fetched, findings listed, exit 1; `main@origin` unchanged |
| Same, with `--rebase` | fetched and rebased, exit 0 |
| Remote rewrote the tip, no local work | followed the rewrite, exit 0 |
| Remote rewrote the tip under an edited file | not fetched, file untouched, exit 1 |
| This workspace, `--scope=both` | agent-repo up to date; work-repo held for its uncommitted changes, exit 1 |

**Things to check when you review**
- **One deviation from what I proposed.** I said I'd count every local-only commit, bookmarked or not. I did not: this repo holds three unbookmarked leftovers from the bookmarks deleted this morning, and counting them would hold the repo back permanently. The check is your original three.
- **Breaking changes.** A repo that is ahead, or has uncommitted changes, used to be synced and is now held back with a non-zero exit. That includes the last line of the table: an acquaint mid-cycle will see exit 1 for the work-repo.
- **The prompt is gone.** On a terminal sync used to ask before rebasing a dirty `@`; now `--rebase` is the only way to say yes.
- **A held repo's report doesn't say whether the remote also moved,** since sync didn't ask it.
- **No new `unwrap` or `expect`** in non-test code.

**The `--undo` rung.** With the gate, the only thing left to undo is a sync you forced with `--rebase`. I've left the rung in the ladder, with a note that whether it is still wanted is your call. The tested restore code from the earlier draft is saved in `tmp/rung1-restore-draft/` if it is.

**Record:** `zDOING.md` is rewritten for this design: the Todo text, Solution, Acceptance check with results, the three-rung ladder with this rung's write-up, and a Deliberation listing the three designs the gate replaced.

content.text:
Both fit the gate design, and each has one thing to settle.

**`--undo`**

I agree it should stay. The gate keeps the routine sync from doing harm, but `--rebase` deliberately goes past the gate, and that is exactly where things can go wrong: a rebase with conflicts, or a rebased `@` you didn't want. That path needs a way back.

- **The hard part is already done.** The restore I wrote and tested earlier puts back bookmarks, `@`, files, and git's remote-tracking refs. It is saved and can go straight into the rung.
- **Finding what to undo.** Sync would label its jj operations so `--undo` can find where the last run started, with nothing stored on disk between runs.
- **When it refuses.** If anything other than sync's own operations came after, `--undo` refuses and says why, so it can't discard later work.
- **The conversation.** In the agent-repo a restore would rewind files that are being written. So there `--undo` has to carry the writes made since the sync forward onto the restored state, never drop them. jj can do that as a merge, but it is the part I'd want agreed on paper first.

**`--dry-run`**

Also useful, and the gate makes it easier to do safely than my first attempt.

- **The trap to avoid:** a dry run that fetches and then restores. That is the design we just backed out of, with the same risk to the agent-repo.
- **The safe version: ask the remote without fetching.** Git can report which commit a remote's `main` is on without downloading or changing anything. `--dry-run` would print the gate's findings plus that answer:

  | It would say | Meaning |
  |---|---|
  | up to date | remote and local are on the same commit |
  | behind, a sync would follow the remote | the remote moved and there is no local work |
  | ahead | local work, remote unchanged |
  | diverged, a sync needs `--rebase` | local work and the remote moved |

- **It changes nothing at all**: no fetch, no jj operation, no file. Safe mid-conversation and safe for anyone.
- **It also fixes a gap in the rung as it stands.** A held repo's report currently can't say whether the remote also moved. With this it can.
- **What it can't tell:** "behind" from "the remote rewrote a commit", since it never downloads the commits. Both are reported as "the remote moved".
- **One thing to verify:** how to ask the remote from our code. jj's fetch already runs `git` underneath, so the ability exists, but I haven't checked how it is exposed.

**How I'd fit them in**

The ladder would become four commits: the gate (done, at review), `--dry-run`, `--undo`, closing. The acquaint and cycle-start rules in the parked v0.2.8 would then name `vc-x1 sync --scope=both --dry-run` for the look.

Before committing to the `--dry-run` rung I'd spend a few minutes confirming the ask-the-remote call works here, and tell you what I find.

content.text:
I think it's worth doing, and I don't see an issue that would stop it. It costs one extra review-and-push round and makes the cycle five commits.

**Why it's a good idea beyond the shape**
- **Rung 1's diff becomes just the gate.** Right now that commit also carries the `TODO.md` reshuffle and all of the new `zDOING.md`. With an opening, the bookkeeping lands first and rung 1 is code, tests, docs and its own write-up.
- **The bookend pair exists.** `git log --grep "feat: sync is safe by default"` returns the opening and the closing, as for any normal multi-step cycle.
- **The trial has a natural home.** Creating `zDOING.md` and pointing `TODO.md` at it is setup, which is what an opening is for.

**One addition to your list of files**

The opening should also carry `zDOING.md`, not only `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` and `TODO.md`. In this trial the cycle's record lives there, and the opening is the commit that writes the plan. Its ladder would show the opening rung as done and the rest not yet started.

**How I'd do it**

The agent-files already describe this case: set the next rung's edits aside, make the inserted commit by itself, then bring the edits back.
1. Start a fresh working copy on `main`, leaving the rung 1 change as a local commit beside it.
2. Copy `TODO.md` and `zDOING.md` from the rung 1 change, set the manifest to `vc-x1-dev` at the `-0` version, and add the opening rung to the ladder.
3. Validate, review, and push it as `feat: sync is safe by default opening`, with the short pointer body an opening takes.
4. Move the rung 1 change on top of the opening and continue from "please review" with its version at `-1`.

**Risks, all small**
- **Conflicts when the rung 1 change moves onto the opening.** Unlikely, because the opening's files are copied from that change; what remains in rung 1 for those files is the version bump and its own ladder marks.
- **The opening must validate with no code change in it.** It will: it is `main`'s code with a different version string.
- **Rung 1's write-up in `zDOING.md` splits across two commits.** The plan goes in the opening and the "what this rung found" text stays with rung 1. That is how the record is meant to grow anyway.

So the ladder would read: opening, the gate, `--dry-run`, `--undo`, closing, with versions `-0` through `-3` and then the bare version.

Rung 1 is flipped to `(done)` and validation passed after that edit. The description:

**Title**

```
feat: sync fetches only a repo with no local work
```

**Body**

```
A sync, `vc-x1 sync`, fetched whatever repo it was pointed at, and a
fetch is not a harmless look: jj's fetch changes the repo as it
imports. "Local work" is what such a change can collide with:
uncommitted changes in `@`, an `@-` that is not on the remote, or a
bookmark with commits the remote does not have.

* A fetch can damage local work. It leaves a bookmark that diverged
  conflicted, and when the remote rewrote a commit the clone has it
  rebases `@` onto the rewrite, which can leave conflict markers in a
  file.
  - Sync checks each repo for local work first and fetches only a repo
    that holds none, where every commit a fetch can touch is the
    remote's own. The agent repo's `@` is not asked to be empty, since
    it holds the running session.
  - A repo that holds local work is not fetched. Sync lists what it
    found, syncs the other repos, and then fails naming it.
  - With --rebase the repo is synced anyway. The prompt that asked
    before rebasing a non-empty `@` is gone, the flag being the one
    way to say yes.
* After a fetch a repo that was behind reads as up to date, the fetch
  having moved its bookmark.
  - Sync reads each bookmark before the fetch and classifies from
    that.
* A remote that rewrote the local commit read as diverged.
  - It is a state of its own, rewritten, which the fetch has already
    followed.
* An ahead bookmark was reported as up to date.
  - It is reported as ahead, in the per-repo lines.

BREAKING-CHANGE: `vc-x1 sync` no longer fetches a repo that holds
local work. It exits non-zero naming the repo, where it synced a repo
that was ahead or had uncommitted changes, and it no longer prompts:
--rebase syncs such a repo.
```

content.text:
Yes, that is what it amounts to. One `vc-x1 push` does all of it:

1. **Commits the working copy.** The change your `0.84.21-1` bookmark sits on gets the title and body above and becomes the rung 1 commit. Its commit id changes because the description is added, but it is the same change, so `0.84.21-1` stays on it.
2. **Moves `feat-sync-is-safe-by-default`** from the opening up to that commit.
3. **Pushes `feat-sync-is-safe-by-default` to origin.** Only that bookmark is pushed.
4. **Does the same for the agent-repo:** commits the session data to its `main`, pushes it, and stamps each commit with the `ochid:` trailer pointing at the other.

Afterwards both bookmarks point at the same commit, and a new empty working copy sits on top for rung 2:

```
@   (empty)                      <- rung 2 starts here
○   feat: sync fetches only ...  <- feat-sync-is-safe-by-default, 0.84.21-1
○   feat: sync is safe by default opening
◆   main
```

`0.84.21-1` stays local. `vc-x1 push` never pushes a bookmark it wasn't given.

One side effect of the new gate worth knowing: while `0.84.21-1` exists only locally it is not "a bookmark with commits the remote does not have", because the commit it names will be on origin under the cycle bookmark. So it won't cause sync to hold the repo back once this push is done.

# Process-spawn ban, since 0.79.0. The mechanism, the ban as config,
# the grant as an attribute, this comment as the register, is
# explained in README.md under "No process spawns". A new
# `Command::new` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register, closed (wink, 2026-08-19), reopened once for entry 5:
#
# 1. Version gate: the `jj -V` probe (src/version.rs). The gate
#    exists to compare the user's jj CLI against our jj-lib, so the
#    CLI spawn is its subject matter.
# 2. Push's `$EDITOR` launch (src/push.rs): interactive message
#    editing is a spawn by definition.
# 3. Init's gh provisioning (src/init.rs): `gh auth status`,
#    `gh repo view`, `gh repo create`. Creating a repo on GitHub is
#    the forge's REST API, not a version-control operation, and no jj or
#    git library can do it, and gh is GitHub's authenticated client.
# 4. Test helpers (src/test_helpers.rs and tests/common/mod.rs):
#    real-jj/git fixture setup and interop verification, kept
#    deliberately independent of the facade under test, and never a
#    substitute for asserting our jj-lib paths directly. The CLI
#    tests' launcher spawning the built vc-x1 binary is this entry
#    too: spawning the binary is what a CLI test is.
# 5. The validate subcommand (src/validate.rs): runs the
#    workspace's configured `[validate]` commands, which is its
#    whole job. Opened 2026-08-21 by the "empty custom-family into
#    the pinned set and config" cycle, whose plan put the checklist
#    commands in config for one subcommand to run.
#
# jj-lib's own git children (fetch/push/clone network legs, the
# default-branch query) are jj-lib's implementation detail, not
# vc-x1 spawn sites, and no lint here sees them.
disallowed-methods = [
    { path = "std::process::Command::new", reason = "vc-x1 runs jj and git through jj-lib and gix, never by spawning their binaries: a new spawn site needs an entry in the register comment at the top of clippy.toml and a visible #[allow] at the site (README: No process spawns)" },
]

1878:### No process spawns

1880-vc-x1 runs jj and git through the jj-lib and gix libraries, never by spawning the `jj` or `git`
1881-binaries. The ban is enforced, and the exceptions are not: there is no allowlist. What exists is
1882-three things, and it pays to know which is which.
1883-
1884-- **The ban is config.** `clippy.toml` lists `std::process::Command::new` under
1885-  `disallowed-methods`, and `Cargo.toml` sets that lint to deny, so a bare call anywhere fails
1886-  `cargo clippy`, which `vc-x1 validate` runs.
1887-- **An exception is an attribute.** Clippy has no way to list permitted sites, so the only grant
1888-  is `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` on the call itself, with a comment naming the entry
1889-  it claims. Nine sites carry one today.

content.text:
I've hit a rule of yours that I should not work around on my own, so I've stopped. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**What happened**

Validation failed at clippy. My `--dry-run` asks the remote by running `git ls-remote`, and the project bans spawning `jj` or `git`:

> vc-x1 runs jj and git through jj-lib and gix, never by spawning their binaries

The ban has been in force since 0.79.0, and the register of permitted spawns in `clippy.toml` is marked "closed (wink, 2026-08-19), reopened once". It lists five entries, none of them a git call.

I was wrong when I told you this added "no new kind of dependency". I saw that the project runs `jj -V`, `gh` and the editor and assumed a git spawn was the same sort of thing. It isn't: those are the register's named exceptions, and a git spawn is exactly what the ban exists to prevent.

**Where the code stands**
- The look works: all sync tests pass, including four new ones.
- It cannot pass validation as written.
- The code, help text and README edits are in the working copy, uncommitted.

**The options I can see**

1. **Reopen the register for a sixth entry.** Add "sync's remote look (`git ls-remote`)" to `clippy.toml` with its reason, and put the `#[allow]` at the one call site. The honest reason: jj-lib does this same kind of query itself by spawning git, but keeps that layer private, and the Rust git library is built here without a network client. It is the smallest change, but it is your rule to bend, not mine.
2. **Use the Rust git library's network client.** No spawn, so the ban holds. It means enabling extra features on `gix`, which brings in an HTTP transport and its own credential handling. That is more dependencies and build time, and it may not pick up your git credentials the way `git` does. I'd have to try it to know.
3. **Drop the remote query from `--dry-run`.** It would report only the local work it finds, plus how the bookmark stands against the last fetch. It could not say whether the remote has moved since, which is the main thing you'd want from it.
4. **Drop the `--dry-run` rung**, and let the gate be the safety.

I'd lean to option 1 if you're willing to reopen the register, since jj-lib already does the equivalent under the hood, and to option 2 if the ban is firm. Which do you want?

content.text:
Almost. You do already use gix directly in a few places, but always for local work and never to talk to a remote. And one fact bears on the decision: jj-lib itself runs the `git` binary for anything that touches the network.

**Where the project uses gix directly today**

`gix` is a direct dependency in `Cargo.toml`, deliberately with "no features of our own", so it is exactly the gix that jj-lib pulls in. Four uses, all local:
- **`src/init.rs`:** creating a bare git repo.
- **`src/jj.rs`:** reading a remote's URL from the repo's git config, and parsing a URL.
- **`src/jj/session.rs`:** picking the hash kind (sha1 or sha256).
- **`src/jj/session.rs`:** recognising gix's lock-contention error so a retry can be made.

Everything else goes through jj-lib.

**How the network is reached today**

jj-lib does not use gix for the network. For fetch, push and clone it spawns the `git` binary itself. Your `clippy.toml` says so: "jj-lib's own git children (fetch/push/clone network legs, the default-branch query) are jj-lib's implementation detail". So:
- vc-x1's own code never spawns `git`. That is what the ban guarantees.
- A `git` process still runs on every sync and push, started by jj-lib.
- The gix in this build has no network client at all. I checked the resolved features: none of the transport ones are on.

**What that means for option 2**

Enabling gix's network client would be the first time vc-x1 reaches a remote by any route other than jj-lib's. Concretely:
- **A second network path.** A look would go through gix's own HTTP client, while the fetch that follows goes through the `git` binary. They can disagree: different credential handling, proxy settings, and SSH behaviour.
- **Credentials are the main risk.** `git` uses your configured credential helper. gix has its own implementation of that, and I can't say without trying whether it works against your GitHub setup.
- **More to build.** An HTTP transport and TLS stack get added to the dependency tree.
- **The "no features of our own" comment in `Cargo.toml` stops being true**, and the gix version stays pinned to whatever jj-lib resolves.

**What it means for option 1**

A `git ls-remote` spawn would be vc-x1 doing directly what jj-lib already does one layer down, with the same binary, config and credentials as the fetch. It breaks the letter of the ban, not really its purpose, which as I read it is to keep vc-x1 off the `jj` CLI and its text output.

So my lean shifts toward option 1 on reliability grounds, but the ban is yours and you may value keeping it absolute. If you prefer option 2, I'd suggest I first try it against this repo's `origin` and report whether credentials work, before committing the rung to it.

message.content: So jj-lib is using gix for local git repo manipulation, but for network stuff it spawns git and does not use gix?

content.text:
Yes. I checked both halves in the jj-lib 0.45.1 source this build uses.

- **Local work goes through gix.** Reading and writing commits, refs, the index and config in the repo's git store is done in-process with the gix library.
- **Network work spawns `git`.** jj-lib's `git_subprocess.rs` has four functions that start the `git` binary: one each for fetch, push, pruning remote branches, and `git remote show` (the default-branch query).
- **gix has no network client in this build.** jj-lib asks for these gix features only: `attributes`, `blob-diff`, `index`, `max-performance-safe`, `sha1`, `sha256`. None is a transport.

The git binary it runs is the one named by jj's `git.executable-path` setting, which is why fetch and push use your normal git config and credentials.

content.text:
I agree on both counts: it is odd to spawn `git` for something jj-lib is one small step from offering, and if we do it we should make sure we notice when we can stop.

**Why jj-lib could reasonably expose it**
- It already has the machinery: a private layer that runs `git` for fetch, push and the default-branch query.
- The default-branch query is the closest thing it offers publicly, and it returns only a branch name, not the commit a branch is on. "Which commit is the remote's bookmark on, without fetching" is a natural sibling.
- So this would be a small addition for them. I don't know whether an issue for it already exists upstream. I haven't looked, and I'd rather search than guess.

**How I'd track it, cheapest first**
1. **Say so at the spawn itself.** The `clippy.toml` register entry and the comment at the call site would state the condition for removal: "until jj-lib exposes a remote-ref query".
2. **A `## Waiting` entry in `TODO.md`.** That section exists for exactly this: work that can't start yet, with a condition that can be checked. Every cycle opening already checks those conditions. The entry would name the upstream issue once there is one.
3. **A note where the jj-lib version is pinned.** Whoever bumps jj-lib in `Cargo.toml` then sees "check whether the remote-ref query landed" at the moment it matters.
4. **An upstream feature request.** I can search the jj issue tracker for an existing one, and draft the text if there isn't. Posting it is public and under your name, so I'd hand you the draft to post.

**Keeping the swap cheap**

The spawn lives in one function, `ls_remote`, behind the same facade as every other jj call. The tests assert what it returns, not how. When jj-lib offers the query, replacing the body is a one-function change and the register entry closes again.

**One caution on timing**

Even if upstream agrees quickly, it arrives in a future jj-lib release, and this project pins jj-lib and gates on the jj CLI matching it. So the spawn would realistically live for some months either way.

If you settle on option 1, the pieces would be: the sixth register entry, the `#[allow]` at the call, the `## Waiting` entry, and the note at the jj-lib pin, all in this rung. I'd do the upstream search separately and report what I find.

message.content: Why do we have to "pin" jj-lib we're going to be spawning `git` aren't we?

content.text:
We don't have to pin anything new. I worded that badly.

- **jj-lib's version is already fixed in `Cargo.toml`**, as `jj-lib = "0.45"`, because every other jj operation in vc-x1 goes through it. That has nothing to do with this change, and spawning `git ls-remote` doesn't touch it.
- **What I meant by "a note at the jj-lib pin"** was only a comment on that existing line. When someone later raises it to a newer jj-lib, the comment reminds them to check whether jj-lib now offers the remote query, so the `git` spawn can be removed.
- **The "some months" remark** was about the removal, not the spawn. If upstream adds the query, we get it only when the project moves to the jj-lib release that contains it.

So option 1 adds one `git` spawn and some reminders, and changes no dependency.

I checked. jj-lib 0.46.0 is the latest published, and it does not add this. So upgrading would not remove the need for the spawn.

**What 0.46.0 has**
- **No remote-ref query.** There is no `ls-remote` anywhere in its source.
- **The same private git layer.** It still spawns `git` for fetch, push, pruning and the default-branch query, and adds three spawns for git worktrees. None is public.
- **The only public remote question is still the default branch name**, which doesn't give a commit.
- **gix still has no network client.** Same feature list as 0.45, on gix 0.88 instead of 0.87.

**What an upgrade would involve, separately from this**
- Your installed `jj` is 0.45.1, and vc-x1 checks that the `jj` CLI matches the jj-lib it is built with. So moving to jj-lib 0.46 means upgrading `jj` as well.
- gix moves from 0.87 to 0.88, and the `gix` line in `Cargo.toml` has to follow.
- jj-lib's API tends to change between releases, so the facade would likely need edits.

That is a cycle of its own, and since it doesn't help here I'd keep it out of this one. I can add it as a `## Todo` entry if you'd like.

**Where that leaves the decision**

Option 1 (spawn `git ls-remote`, with the register entry and the reminders) is still the way to get `--dry-run` asking the remote. The upstream feature request becomes more worthwhile, since two releases in a row don't have it.

I read 0.46.0 from a copy downloaded into a scratch directory. Nothing in the project changed.

Do you want me to go ahead with option 1?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Acceptance check for `feat: sync --dry-run asks the remote and changes nothing`.
set -uo pipefail
d="$1"
rm -rf "$d"
mkdir -p "$d"
cd "$d" || exit 1
git init -q --bare remote.git
jj git clone --quiet remote.git a
(cd a && echo one > f && jj commit --quiet -m one && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @- \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
for n in b c r2; do jj git clone --quiet remote.git "$n"; done
(cd a && echo two > g && jj commit --quiet -m two && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @- \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
jj git clone --quiet remote.git u
(cd c && echo local > h && jj commit --quiet -m local && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @-)
jj git fetch --quiet -R r2; jj new --quiet main -R r2

state() { jj log -R "$1" --ignore-working-copy -r 'main | @- | main@origin' --no-graph \
  -T 'commit_id.short(8) ++ " " ++ bookmarks ++ " " ++ remote_bookmarks ++ " | " ++ description.first_line() ++ "\n"'; }
ops() { jj op log -R "$1" --ignore-working-copy --no-graph -T 'id.short(8) ++ "\n"' | wc -l; }
look() {
  local before after s0 s1
  before=$(ops "$1"); s0=$(state "$1")
  echo "\$ vc-x1 sync -R $1 --dry-run"
  vc-x1-dev --no-banner sync -R "$1" --dry-run < /dev/null; echo "exit=$?"
  after=$(ops "$1"); s1=$(state "$1")
  echo "operations added: $((after - before)); bookmarks and @ unchanged: $([ "$s0" = "$s1" ] && echo yes || echo NO)"
}

echo "=== up to date"; look u
echo "=== behind"; look b
echo "=== diverged (an unpushed commit, remote moved)"; look c
(cd a && echo rewritten > g && jj squash --quiet --ignore-immutable \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
echo "r2-local-edit" > r2/g
echo "=== remote rewrote its tip, an edited file in @"; look r2; echo "--- r2/g: $(cat r2/g)"

content.text:
No, and the report is misleading there. That's a fault in my wording, and it also exposes a rough edge in the gate.

**What the two lines actually mean**
- **"up-to-date"** is only about the bookmark being synced, `main` by default: your `main` and origin's `main` are on the same commit. The report doesn't even say which bookmark, which is confusing when you're sitting on a cycle bookmark.
- **"holds local work"** is the gate's finding: `docs-capture-the-multi-repo-design-notes` has commits origin doesn't have.

**What a real `vc-x1 sync` would do there**

It would refuse: print the same local-work finding, fetch nothing, and exit non-zero. Nothing would be harmed, but it is not "safe to go ahead" in the sense of "it will sync". The look should have said that outright.

**Fix 1, wording (I'd do this now, in this rung)**

Name the bookmark and end each repo with a plain verdict:

```
.: main is up to date with origin
.: holds local work:
.:   bookmark docs-capture-the-multi-repo-design-notes has commits origin does not
.: a sync would be held back: push the local work, or pass --rebase
```

The verdict line would be one of: nothing to do, would follow the remote, would be held back, needs `--rebase`.

**Fix 2, behaviour (your call)**

Your case shows a cost of the "every bookmark fast-forward only" check: one unpushed bookmark anywhere in the repo holds every sync back, even when origin hasn't changed and a fetch would bring nothing.

Now that sync can ask the remote without fetching, it could do that first:
- **Origin hasn't moved since the last fetch:** there is nothing to fetch, so nothing can collide. Sync reports "up to date", notes the local work, and exits 0.
- **Origin has moved and the repo holds local work:** held back, as now.

That keeps the protection exactly where a fetch could do harm and stops the gate from nagging when it can't. To be sound it has to compare all of origin's bookmarks with what was last fetched, not only `main`, because a fetch brings all of them.

The cost is that every sync then makes the `git ls-remote` call, so the spawn exception becomes part of the routine path, not just `--dry-run`.

I recommend both fixes. Fix 1 belongs in this rung. Fix 2 changes rung 1's behaviour, so I'd make it a rung of its own after this one, unless you'd rather fold it in here. Which do you want?

message.content: I agree, but isn't also safe to sync, nothing would be lost?

content.text:
Yes. In your iiac-perf case a sync would be completely safe: origin's `main` hasn't moved, so a fetch would bring nothing, and nothing can collide with that unpushed bookmark. The gate holding it back there is over-cautious, and that is exactly what Fix 2 removes.

It's worth being precise about what the gate protects, because "lost" is a strong word:

- **jj never loses commits.** Even in the bad cases, everything stays in the repo and its operation log.
- **What the gate prevents is a tangle.** A fetch can leave a bookmark conflicted, or rebase your unpushed commits onto a rewritten remote and leave conflict markers in files. That is recoverable but confusing, especially for someone without help.
- **A tangle needs the remote to have moved.** If origin is where it was at the last fetch, there is nothing for local work to collide with.

So the honest rule is the one Fix 2 implements:
- **Remote unchanged:** sync has nothing to do. It says so, mentions the local work as a note, and exits 0.
- **Remote moved, no local work:** fetch and follow it.
- **Remote moved, and local work present:** held back, because sync can't tell an ordinary advance from a rewrite without downloading the commits.

One refinement falls out of your example. A bookmark that was never pushed has no remote counterpart, so even when origin has moved, a fetch only touches it if origin rewrote a commit underneath it. That is rare, but sync can't rule it out without fetching, so I'd still hold in that case.

Shall I go ahead with both: Fix 1 (clearer wording with the bookmark named and a verdict line) in this rung, and Fix 2 (ask the remote first, hold only when it has moved) as the next rung?

message.content: go, both fixes. But we "must" be able to sync and even if it wasn't "safe" we still must allow the user to force a sync if they want to, correct?

content.text:
Correct, and that already exists: `--rebase` is the force. It skips the gate entirely, fetches, and rebases whatever needs it, so a user can always sync if they choose to. The look's verdict line will say so wherever a sync would be held back.

One naming thought, for later if you want it: `--rebase` describes what it does once past the gate, but "force a sync" may be how people think of it. An alias such as `--force` would be cheap to add.

Now doing Fix 1 in this rung, and adding Fix 2 to the ladder as the next rung.

content.text:
Good questions; both expose something that reads wrong.

**Why "rebase"?**

Only because that is the name of the flag that gets past the gate. `--rebase` means "sync this repo even though it holds local work, and rebase whatever turns out to need it". In your iiac-perf case nothing would need rebasing: the flag would just unlock the gate, sync would find nothing to fetch, and it would finish. So the word is misleading there, which is the case for calling it `--force`.

**Why "held back" when it's up to date?**

Because the look knows more than the real sync does today.

- The real sync, as pushed in rung 1, checks for local work *before* it contacts the remote. At that moment it doesn't know whether anything would come down, so it refuses on local work alone.
- The look does contact the remote, so it can see `main` is up to date. Its verdict then reports honestly what the real sync would do, which is refuse.

So the line is accurate about current behaviour, and the behaviour is what's silly: you're right that with nothing coming down there is nothing to hold back for.

**Fix 2 is what removes it.** After that rung the real sync asks the remote first, and your case becomes:

```
.: 'main' is up to date with origin
.: holds local work:
.:   bookmark docs-capture-the-multi-repo-design-notes has commits origin does not
.: a sync would have nothing to do
```

and a real `vc-x1 sync` there exits 0. "Held back" would appear only when the remote has actually moved and there is local work.

content.text:
Your instinct is right on the second point, with one exception, and that exception is exactly what the first question is about.

**Is uncommitted work safe when we're behind?**

It depends on how the remote moved:
- **The remote added commits on top (a fast-forward).** A fetch moves the `main` bookmark forward and does not touch `@`. Your uncommitted work stays where it is, on the old commit, undisturbed. Sync then leaves a non-empty `@` in place unless told to rebase it. So yes, safe.
- **The remote replaced a commit you're sitting on (a forced push).** A fetch rebases `@` onto the replacement, and edits to the same lines become conflict markers. This is the one case that disturbs uncommitted work.

The same holds for unpushed commits on some other bookmark: a fast-forward of `main` never touches them; only a rewrite underneath them does.

So "behind" is safe for local work precisely when the move is a fast-forward. In this project a landed `main` is never rewritten, so for `main` it is always a fast-forward in practice. Rewrites happen to the agent-repo's tip (`squash-push` from another machine) and to cycle bookmarks that get amended.

**Can we tell a fast-forward from a rewrite before syncing?**

Not with what the look does today. `git ls-remote` returns only the commit id the remote is on. When that commit isn't in the repo yet, there is no way to ask whether it descends from yours.

It can be determined with one more step: download the remote's new commits without moving any bookmark, then check ancestry locally.
- Git can fetch commits into the object store while leaving every branch and remote-tracking ref alone. jj only reacts to refs, so it would not notice.
- With the commits present, "is my commit an ancestor of theirs" is a local question, which the Rust git library can answer in-process. No further spawn.
- The result is exact: fast-forward, rewrite, or diverged, per bookmark.

I have not tested that download step. Git has a habit of updating remote-tracking refs as a side effect of a fetch, which would defeat the purpose, so I'd verify it in a scratch repo first, as I did with `ls-remote`.

**What that would let the gate become**

Instead of "the remote moved and you have local work, so hold back", it could be precise:
- **Fast-forward:** proceed. Bookmarks move, uncommitted work and unrelated unpushed commits are left alone, and the report says so.
- **A rewrite under local work, or the synced bookmark itself diverged:** hold back, naming which.

That is the rule you're describing, and it would make "held back" rare and always meaningful.

**How I'd fit it in**

This is a richer version of Fix 2. I'd make it the content of that rung: ask the remote, and when it has moved, download without moving anything and classify exactly. If the download step turns out not to be clean, the fallback is the simpler Fix 2 (hold whenever the remote moved and there is local work).

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Can git download a remote's new commits without moving any ref, so
# jj notices nothing, and can ancestry then be asked locally?
set -uo pipefail
d="$1"
rm -rf "$d"
mkdir -p "$d"
cd "$d" || exit 1
git init -q --bare remote.git
jj git clone --quiet --colocate remote.git a
(cd a && echo one > f && jj commit --quiet -m one && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @- \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
jj git clone --quiet --colocate remote.git ff      # will see a fast-forward
jj git clone --quiet --colocate remote.git rw      # will see a rewrite
jj git clone --quiet --no-colocate remote.git nc   # non-colocated, sees a fast-forward

refs() { git --git-dir "$1" for-each-ref --format='%(refname) %(objectname:short=8)' refs/remotes refs/heads; }
jjstate() { jj log -R "$1" -r 'main | @- | main@origin' --no-graph \
  -T 'commit_id.short(8) ++ " " ++ bookmarks ++ " " ++ remote_bookmarks ++ "\n"'; }
nops() { jj op log -R "$1" --ignore-working-copy --no-graph -T 'id.short(8) ++ "\n"' | wc -l; }

probe() {  # probe <repo> <git-dir>
  local repo="$1" gd="$2" theirs mine r0 r1 o0 o1 j0 j1
  mine=$(git --git-dir "$gd" rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main)
  theirs=$(git --git-dir "$gd" ls-remote origin refs/heads/main | cut -f1)
  echo "last fetched ${mine:0:8}, remote now ${theirs:0:8}"
  echo "have their commit before: $(git --git-dir "$gd" cat-file -e "$theirs" 2>/dev/null && echo yes || echo no)"
  r0=$(refs "$gd"); o0=$(nops "$repo"); j0=$(jjstate "$repo")
  git --git-dir "$gd" fetch --quiet --refmap= --no-tags --no-write-fetch-head origin refs/heads/main
  echo "download exit=$?"
  echo "have their commit after:  $(git --git-dir "$gd" cat-file -e "$theirs" 2>/dev/null && echo yes || echo no)"
  r1=$(refs "$gd")
  echo "git refs unchanged: $([ "$r0" = "$r1" ] && echo yes || echo NO)"
  # Any jj command imports git refs in a colocated repo: does jj see a change?
  jj st -R "$repo" > /dev/null 2>&1
  j1=$(jjstate "$repo"); o1=$(nops "$repo")
  echo "jj bookmarks, @, main@origin unchanged: $([ "$j0" = "$j1" ] && echo yes || echo NO); jj operations added: $((o1 - o0))"
  if git --git-dir "$gd" merge-base --is-ancestor "$mine" "$theirs"; then
    echo "ancestry: last-fetched is an ancestor of the remote's -> FAST-FORWARD"
  else
    echo "ancestry: last-fetched is NOT an ancestor of the remote's -> REWRITE"
  fi
}

# The remote advances: ff and nc are behind by a fast-forward.
(cd a && echo two > g && jj commit --quiet -m two && jj bookmark set --quiet main -r @- \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
echo "=== fast-forward, colocated";     probe ff ff/.git
echo "=== fast-forward, non-colocated"; probe nc nc/.jj/repo/store/git

# rw catches up, then the remote rewrites its tip.
jj git fetch --quiet -R rw; jj new --quiet main -R rw
(cd a && echo rewritten > g && jj squash --quiet --ignore-immutable \
  && jj git push --quiet --bookmark main)
echo "=== rewrite, colocated"; probe rw rw/.git

content.text:
The download-without-moving step works cleanly, in all three cases I tried.

**What I tested**

In scratch clones, with the remote moved after the clone last fetched:

| Case | Had their commit before | After the download | Git refs | jj bookmarks, `@`, `main@origin` | jj operations added | Ancestry answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fast-forward, colocated repo | no | yes | unchanged | unchanged | 0 | fast-forward |
| Fast-forward, non-colocated repo | no | yes | unchanged | unchanged | 0 | fast-forward |
| Remote rewrote its tip | no | yes | unchanged | unchanged | 0 | rewrite |

So git can bring the remote's new commits into the repo's object store while leaving every branch and remote-tracking ref where it was, and jj notices nothing, even after a later jj command that imports git refs.

**How it's done**
- One `git fetch` with three flags: one that stops git updating remote-tracking refs as a side effect (the habit I was worried about), one that skips tags, and one that skips writing `FETCH_HEAD`.
- The ancestry check after that is local. I confirmed the Rust git library as built here can walk history in-process, so it needs no extra spawn and no new library features.

**What it costs**
- **A second kind of `git` spawn**, under the same register entry: `ls-remote` to see whether the remote moved, then this download only when it has.
- **The repo's object store grows** by the remote's new commits. They are the same objects the real fetch would bring moments later, so nothing is wasted when a sync follows.
- **Only the bookmarks asked about are classified.** To be sound for a real sync, it has to cover every bookmark the remote has, since a fetch brings all of them.

**What it makes possible**

The gate can be exact, for the real sync and for the look alike:
- **Fast-forward:** proceed, and say that local work is untouched.
- **Rewrite under local work, or the synced bookmark diverged:** hold back, naming which bookmark and why.
- **Remote unchanged:** nothing to do.

**Suggested plan**
- **This rung (3):** commit `--dry-run` as it stands, with the bookmark named and the verdict line. Its verdict still says "held back" for your iiac-perf case, because that is what the pushed sync does.
- **Rung 4:** the exact gate described above, used by both sync and the look, plus `--force` with `--rebase` kept as an alias. After it, your iiac-perf case reads "a sync would have nothing to do".

Shall I proceed that way, with rung 3 going to its description now?

content.text:
Then we'd say a sync would go ahead, and that the local work is left alone. That is what rung 4 makes possible; today's code would still say "held back".

**The report in that case, after rung 4**

```
.: 'main' is behind origin by a fast-forward (local 1f2e8188, remote 0e62ea24)
.: holds local work:
.:   bookmark docs-capture-the-multi-repo-design-notes has commits origin does not
.: a sync would follow origin and leave the local work untouched
```

And the real `vc-x1 sync` would do exactly that: fetch, move `main` forward, exit 0, and end with a line saying which local work it left untouched.

**Why "untouched" can be stated, not just hoped**

A fast-forward only adds commits on top of what you already have. It replaces nothing. Your unpushed bookmark's commits, and every commit beneath them, are the same before and after, so a fetch has no reason to move or rebase them. Once we've downloaded the remote's commits and confirmed every bookmark the remote moved is a fast-forward, that is a fact about the repo, not a guess.

**What "untouched" does not mean**

It doesn't mean brought up to date. If that bookmark, or an `@` with uncommitted edits, sits on the old `main`, it stays on the old `main`. Sync would say so, for example:

```
.: @ has uncommitted changes and stays on the old 'main'; rebase it when you're ready
```

Moving your own work onto the new `main` is your decision, made with `--force` or by hand.

**Where the "as far as we can tell" really applies**

Only to timing. The look reports the remote as it was when asked, and the remote could move again before you run the sync. The real sync doesn't rely on an earlier look: it asks, downloads, classifies and acts in one run.

**When we'd still say "held back"**
- The remote rewrote a commit that your local work sits on.
- The bookmark being synced has itself diverged: you have commits on it and so does the remote.

In both the verdict would name the bookmark and the reason.

So the plan stands as I laid it out: rung 3 commits `--dry-run` as it is now, and rung 4 brings the exact classification, these verdicts, and `--force`. Shall I take rung 3 to its description?

content.text:
I think a legend is a good idea, and I'd keep it to one line.

**Why it helps**
- The `*` and `-` convention is defined in the agent-files, which a reader of `git log` or GitHub never sees. To them it's just a nested list, and the pairing of problem and solution is easy to miss.
- A legend makes each commit explain itself, wherever it's read.

**What it costs**
- It repeats in every commit that has a list. One line is tolerable; your two-line version would add three lines with its blank line, to every body.

**A one-line form**

```
Legend: `*` is a problem this commit addresses, `-` is a solution to it.
```

file.content:
- One push is one agent-repo commit on its `main`, paired with the work-repo commit, whatever
    bookmark the work-repo is on.
  - Never create an agent-repo bookmark mirroring a work-repo one: it steers session pushes at
    the wrong remote ref.
- **Squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a pass.
  - The agent keeps writing session data while the command runs, so its own record lands after
    the squash.
  - Session data is append-only, so a re-run never conflicts.
  - A single pass is never guaranteed to leave `@` empty.

A late work-repo tweak after the push (a forgotten edit) needs `jj squash --ignore-immutable` and a
re-push, which is a remote rewrite and takes approval like any push.

## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
coordinating with everyone involved first**
([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
covered. That is a [local
ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.

When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

feat: sync --dry-run looks and changes nothing

A sync that holds a repo back for its local work cannot say whether
the remote moved too, and there was no way to learn what a sync would
do without running one. A "look" is that question answered with the
repo left as it is: no fetch, and no bookmark, `@`, or remote-tracking
ref moved.

* A look that fetched would change the repo, a fetch being what moves
  bookmarks and rebases `@`.
  - With --dry-run sync asks each remote which commit its bookmark is
    on, by `git ls-remote`, and downloads nothing.
* The remote's commit may be one the repo does not have, so ancestry
  cannot always be asked.
  - A local bookmark that is on the remote holds nothing of its own
    and reads as behind, and one that is not reads as diverged. A
    remote that advanced and one that rewrote history read the same.
* A state alone leaves the reader to work out what a sync would do,
  and "up to date" over an unpushed bookmark read as "safe to sync".
  - The report names the bookmark, lists the local work found, and
    ends each repo with a verdict: nothing to do, follow the remote,
    rebase, or held back with the way past it.
* The remote is asked by spawning git, which the project bans.
  - The spawn register takes a sixth entry, temporary, for this one
    call: jj-lib has no such query, keeps its own git spawns private,
    and builds gix with no network client.
  - A Waiting entry, a note at the jj-lib dependency, and the comment
    at the call say when the entry closes.
